Such neural tube defects affect nearly 300,000 babies worldwide each year, with the most common types of this condition resulting in parts of the brain or spinal cord being exposed at birth. 1 Since the defects happen in fetuses within the first month of pregnancy often before a person knows they are pregnant, the condition is technically challenging to study in human embryos .  Given the similarity in neural tube development in humans and quails, the animal model comes in handy in investigating this process By using confocal microscopy, White, Tan and their colleagues image quail embryos, shedding light on the molecular dynamics involved in neural tube development. 2 This could offer crucial information about potential therapeutic targets and genes to screen for predicting neural tube defects Continue reading below... Siew Zhuan Tan and Melanie White, UQ Institute for Molecular Bioscience So, she races against time to ensure that the fixed tissue sits comfortably within the gel before it solidifies. She also has to ensure that the sample does not detach from the gel, so she performs whole-mount immunostaining with fluorescent antibodies on the intact sample to prevent separation between the sample and gel on more fragile cut sections. Once this step is done, she slices the tissue to obtain sections almost as thin as a human hair. This usually results in stunning images highlighting the transcriptional regulators and molecules that drive vertebrate neural tube formation. Image credit: © iStock.com, koto_feja , Adapted by Erin Lemieux PDF version Share T he ability to rewind a cell’s biological clock to the point at which it could become any other kind of cell has made stem cell research a sought-after way to better understand developmental biology and establish cell therapies to treat diseases. For years, stem cell researchers used embryonic stem cells to address their research questions, but this opened up the field to ethical concerns, specifically in the use of human embryonic stem cells. But the discovery of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), which are adult somatic cells that can be reprogrammed to give rise to all cells of the body, revolutionized the field. From the announcement of the Yamanaka factors to their use in multiple late-stage clinical trials, iPSCs have changed what’s possible in biomedical science. In celebration of The Scientist’s 40 th anniversary , we searched through our archives to highlight our coverage of the biggest iPSC news over the years. 2006: Publication of the Yamanaka Factors In the spring of 2006, stem cell researcher Shinya Yamanaka , then at Kyoto University and the Japan Science and Technology Agency, presented at a conference that he had identified four unnamed factors that could convert a mouse fibroblast into a pluripotent stem cell. He admitted that one factor was Oct4, but then said, “I'm not brave enough to tell the other three.” Just a few months later in August, he and his colleague, stem cell biologist Kazutoshi Takahashi then of Kyoto University, published the four factors in Cell : Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4. 1 Continue reading below... Yamanaka and his team delivered the four Yamanaka factors to human skin cells using retrovirus-mediated transfection to convert them into iPSCs. They then differentiated these iPSCs into human neural and cardiac cells. 2 The second group—led by University of Wisconsin, Madison stem cell biologist James Thomson —used a lentivirus to deliver a different combination of four transcription factors: Oct4, Sox2, Nanog, and Lin28. 3 The two groups’ findings spurred excitement throughout the research community. Thomson predicted that while human embryonic stem cell research would likely not end, many labs would shift their focus to iPSCs. Many researchers noted that the method still had limitations, such as using retroviruses to deliver the transcription factors, but there was now a proof-of-concept for iPSCs in higher mammals. 2008: The First Patient-Derived iPSCs For the first time, scientists reprogrammed cells from a patient with a disease—amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)—into iPSCs. The team then differentiated these stem cells into healthy motor neurons. While researchers said that this feat was a “stunning accomplishment,” they also noted several limitations, including whether the neurons eventually developed ALS pathology or whether they could make connections with muscle fibers in vivo. However, the researchers were hopeful that these patient-derived iPSCs would help them understand the molecular mechanism underlying ALS and enable them to develop therapeutic compounds to help counteract the disease. It's Trivia Time! Test your iPSC knowledge. 2009: No Need for DNA: Proteins Can Reprogram iPSCs Inserting foreign DNA into cells carries the risk of the DNA integrating into the genome, which can lead to disease-causing genetic modifications. This was especially the case for Yamanaka’s method of producing iPSCs by delivering the four transcription factors via a retrovirus. In the years since then, other researchers developed methods to deliver the factors to cells without integrating DNA into the genome—non-integrating adenoviruses, transient plasmids, and a piggyBac transposon system—but these all still relied on using DNA. In 2009, pharmaceutical chemist Sheng Ding , who was then at the Scripps Research Institute, and his team developed a completely protein-based method to generate iPSCs. They purified the protein versions of the four Yamanaka factors and combined them with the histone deacetylase inhibitor valproic acid to reprogram mouse embryonic fibroblasts into iPSCs. Other stem cell researchers touted the findings as a safer way to create iPSCs, which would make them more viable as therapeutics in the clinic. 2012: Cell Re-Programmers Win the Nobel Prize Just six years after the initial discovery of the factors needed to create iPSCs, Yamanaka and developmental biologist John Gurdon of the Gurdon Institute won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work showing that adult cells could be reprogrammed into pluripotent ones. “Gurdon and Yamanaka fundamentally changed the way we all think about the specialized state of cells,” George Daley , director of the Stem Cell Transplantation Program at the Harvard Medical School, told The Scientist at the time. Gurdon, who was often called “the godfather of cloning,” showed that transferring a nucleus from an adult frog cell into a frog egg led to a cloned tadpole, suggesting that adult cells still had the capacity to undergo embryonic development and differentiate into other cell types. Yamanaka’s discovery of the four factors needed to reprogram adult cells into iPSCs showed that this hypothetical was true. Continue reading below... Read More 2014: First iPSC-Based Clinical Trials Begin for Macular Degeneration With the success of iPSCs in preclinical studies, researchers began developing iPSC-based treatments for patients. In 2013, researchers in Japan initiated the first clinical trial using iPSCs for people with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In this condition, retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the retina’s support cells, are lost, which eventually leads to blindness. In the Japanese trial, the researchers took skin cells from six people with AMD, reprogrammed them into iPSCs, and injected the patient’s own iPSCs into their retinas. Similar trials for AMD also began in the United States. Many of these focused on supplying stem cell-derived RPE cells to support the retina to prevent vision loss. 2014: iPSC Banks Store Patient-Derived Cell Lines As iPSC research continued to grow, stem cell banks for iPSCs derived from patients with different conditions—from Alzheimer’s disease to cardiomyopathy—began to pop up. In particular, when researchers discovered that, in addition to skin cells, white blood cells could also be reprogramed into iPSCs, it led to the opportunity to store patient-derived lymphocytes in massive iPSC banks. The main question on researchers’ minds, though, was economics: How much would storage and maintenance cost the facility, and how much would researchers be able to spend to purchase cell lines? While most banks focused on storing iPSCs for basic research, disease modeling, and drug testing, many researchers hoped that banks with iPSC-based cell therapies would come next. 2018: Multiple iPSC Therapies Enter Clinical Trials Just twelve years after their development, iPSCs had entered clinical trials to treat conditions as diverse as Parkinson’s disease, endometriosis, and spinal cord injury in addition to the earlier trials in heart disease and macular degeneration. To reach this point, teams had to overcome a number of barriers including ensuring that the iPSC-derived cells engrafted well and were efficacious in vivo while also taking care that the cells didn’t lead to cancer formation. Researchers also began exploring “off-the-shelf” iPSC-based therapies. One such therapy reprogrammed donor iPSCs into mesenchymal stem cells, which don’t express donor-specific antigens, lessening the risk of immune rejection. These kinds of therapies are also less expensive to produce than iPSC therapies made from individual patients’ own cells. 2025: Oct4 and the Future of iPSCs Oct4 gained prominence as one of the four Yamanaka factors required for pluripotency, but originally, molecular biologist Hans Schöler , then at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysical Chemistry, had identified it as a transcription factor that bound an eight-letter repeat in DNA. He found that Oct4 played an important role in early development and in maintaining pluripotency. For years, researchers thought Oct4 was the most important of the four Yamanaka factors, but in 2019, Sergiy Velychko , a graduate student in Schöler’s group, found that Oct4 actually wasn’t needed to produce iPSCs. 4 They reported that the reprogramming process took longer, but the resulting cells were of higher quality. They discovered that if they created a more stable Oct4-Sox2 dimer by mutating a residue in Sox2, they could generate more human iPSCs, even from cell types that had been difficult or impossible to reprogram before. Now, other researchers are exploring which parts of Oct4 are most important for reprogramming to potentially create synthetic reprogramming factors as well as looking to artificial intelligence models to further optimize iPSC development. Other stem cell researchers touted the findings as a safer way to create iPSCs, which would make them more viable as therapeutics in the clinic. 2012: Cell Re-Programmers Win the Nobel Prize Just six years after the initial discovery of the factors needed to create iPSCs, Yamanaka and developmental biologist John Gurdon of the Gurdon Institute won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work showing that adult cells could be reprogrammed into pluripotent ones. “Gurdon and Yamanaka fundamentally changed the way we all think about the specialized state of cells,” George Daley , director of the Stem Cell Transplantation Program at the Harvard Medical School, told The Scientist at the time. Gurdon, who was often called “the godfather of cloning,” showed that transferring a nucleus from an adult frog cell into a frog egg led to a cloned tadpole, suggesting that adult cells still had the capacity to undergo embryonic development and differentiate into other cell types. Yamanaka’s discovery of the four factors needed to reprogram adult cells into iPSCs showed that this hypothetical was true. Continue reading below... In this condition, retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, the retina’s support cells, are lost, which eventually leads to blindness. In the Japanese trial, the researchers took skin cells from six people with AMD, reprogrammed them into iPSCs, and injected the patient’s own iPSCs into their retinas. The main question on researchers’ minds, though, was economics: How much would storage and maintenance cost the facility, and how much would researchers be able to spend to purchase cell lines? One such therapy reprogrammed donor iPSCs into mesenchymal stem cells, which don’t express donor-specific antigens, lessening the risk of immune rejection. Thursday, March 26, 2026 11:00 AM-12:00 PM ET Biotherapeutic pipelines don’t just juggle monoclonal antibodies anymore, they need to be ready for protein conjugates like ADCs and for teeny tiny peptides. Even beyond new modalities, automation is pushing throughput higher so that analytical tools for concentration and sizing need to read lots of samples as fast as possible, on the tiniest sample volumes, and with increasingly higher throughput. For ADCs, UV/Vis gets messy when payload absorbance overlaps the antibody signal, and aggregation risk increases as hydrophobic drug-linkers enter the mix. For peptides, answering the questions “How much do I have?” and “Has aggregation struck?” need to happen without turning characterization into a bottleneck. Stunner bundles quantification and sizing checks into a single read that can pinpoint sample concentration and raise the red flag when aggregation has struck. Full-spectrum UV/Vis quantifies while dynamic light scattering (DLS) checks size and aggregation on the same 2 µL sample in a 96-well plate-based format. Stunner’s Unmix algorithms power applications to deconvolute UV/Vis spectra into protein, drug-linkers, nucleic acids, or other components, making quantification and drug-antibody ratio (DAR) reads simpler than ever. Since UV/Vis is read in the same run as DLS, Stunner streamlines workflows for proteins, ADCs, and peptides with less handoffs and variability. In this webinar, brought to you by Unchained Labs, Kevin Lance will discuss how Stunner accelerates everything from routine sample checks and screening to final quality control across protein modalities. Kevin will present the technology behind rapid concentration and aggregation monitoring for proteins and peptides and the newest applications for fast DAR and concentration readouts for ADCs and other conjugates. Overall, this practical guidance will enable the identification of problematic samples and the knowledge to develop faster, sample-sparing, and downstream-friendly methods on Stunner. Image credit: © iStock.com, koto_feja , Adapted by Erin Lemieux PDF version Share T he ability to rewind a cell’s biological clock to the point at which it could become any other kind of cell has made stem cell research a sought-after way to better understand developmental biology and establish cell therapies to treat diseases. For years, stem cell researchers used embryonic stem cells to address their research questions, but this opened up the field to ethical concerns, specifically in the use of human embryonic stem cells. But the discovery of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), which are adult somatic cells that can be reprogrammed to give rise to all cells of the body, revolutionized the field. From the announcement of the Yamanaka factors to their use in multiple late-stage clinical trials, iPSCs have changed what’s possible in biomedical science. In celebration of The Scientist’s 40 th anniversary , we searched through our archives to highlight our coverage of the biggest iPSC news over the years. 2006: Publication of the Yamanaka Factors In the spring of 2006, stem cell researcher Shinya Yamanaka , then at Kyoto University and the Japan Science and Technology Agency, presented at a conference that he had identified four unnamed factors that could convert a mouse fibroblast into a pluripotent stem cell. He admitted that one factor was Oct4, but then said, “I'm not brave enough to tell the other three.” Just a few months later in August, he and his colleague, stem cell biologist Kazutoshi Takahashi then of Kyoto University, published the four factors in Cell : Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4. 1 Continue reading below... Yamanaka and his team delivered the four Yamanaka factors to human skin cells using retrovirus-mediated transfection to convert them into iPSCs. They then differentiated these iPSCs into human neural and cardiac cells. 2 The second group—led by University of Wisconsin, Madison stem cell biologist James Thomson —used a lentivirus to deliver a different combination of four transcription factors: Oct4, Sox2, Nanog, and Lin28. 3 The two groups’ findings spurred excitement throughout the research community. Thomson predicted that while human embryonic stem cell research would likely not end, many labs would shift their focus to iPSCs. Many researchers noted that the method still had limitations, such as using retroviruses to deliver the transcription factors, but there was now a proof-of-concept for iPSCs in higher mammals. 2008: The First Patient-Derived iPSCs For the first time, scientists reprogrammed cells from a patient with a disease—amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)—into iPSCs. The team then differentiated these stem cells into healthy motor neurons. While researchers said that this feat was a “stunning accomplishment,” they also noted several limitations, including whether the neurons eventually developed ALS pathology or whether they could make connections with muscle fibers in vivo. However, the researchers were hopeful that these patient-derived iPSCs would help them understand the molecular mechanism underlying ALS and enable them to develop therapeutic compounds to help counteract the disease. Test your iPSC knowledge. 2009: No Need for DNA: Proteins Can Reprogram iPSCs Inserting foreign DNA into cells carries the risk of the DNA integrating into the genome, which can lead to disease-causing genetic modifications. This was especially the case for Yamanaka’s method of producing iPSCs by delivering the four transcription factors via a retrovirus. In the years since then, other researchers developed methods to deliver the factors to cells without integrating DNA into the genome—non-integrating adenoviruses, transient plasmids, and a piggyBac transposon system—but these all still relied on using DNA. In 2009, pharmaceutical chemist Sheng Ding , who was then at the Scripps Research Institute, and his team developed a completely protein-based method to generate iPSCs. They purified the protein versions of the four Yamanaka factors and combined them with the histone deacetylase inhibitor valproic acid to reprogram mouse embryonic fibroblasts into iPSCs. Other stem cell researchers touted the findings as a safer way to create iPSCs, which would make them more viable as therapeutics in the clinic. 2012: Cell Re-Programmers Win the Nobel Prize Just six years after the initial discovery of the factors needed to create iPSCs, Yamanaka and developmental biologist John Gurdon of the Gurdon Institute won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work showing that adult cells could be reprogrammed into pluripotent ones. “Gurdon and Yamanaka fundamentally changed the way we all think about the specialized state of cells,” George Daley , director of the Stem Cell Transplantation Program at the Harvard Medical School, told The Scientist at the time. Gurdon, who was often called “the godfather of cloning,” showed that transferring a nucleus from an adult frog cell into a frog egg led to a cloned tadpole, suggesting that adult cells still had the capacity to undergo embryonic development and differentiate into other cell types. Yamanaka’s discovery of the four factors needed to reprogram adult cells into iPSCs showed that this hypothetical was true. Continue reading below... In the Japanese trial, the researchers took skin cells from six people with AMD, reprogrammed them into iPSCs, and injected the patient’s own iPSCs into their retinas. Similar trials for AMD also began in the United States. Many of these focused on supplying stem cell-derived RPE cells to support the retina to prevent vision loss. 2014: iPSC Banks Store Patient-Derived Cell Lines As iPSC research continued to grow, stem cell banks for iPSCs derived from patients with different conditions—from Alzheimer’s disease to cardiomyopathy—began to pop up. In particular, when researchers discovered that, in addition to skin cells, white blood cells could also be reprogramed into iPSCs, it led to the opportunity to store patient-derived lymphocytes in massive iPSC banks. The main question on researchers’ minds, though, was economics: How much would storage and maintenance cost the facility, and how much would researchers be able to spend to purchase cell lines? To reach this point, teams had to overcome a number of barriers including ensuring that the iPSC-derived cells engrafted well and were efficacious in vivo while also taking care that the cells didn’t lead to cancer formation. Researchers also began exploring “off-the-shelf” iPSC-based therapies. He found that Oct4 played an important role in early development and in maintaining pluripotency. For years, researchers thought Oct4 was the most important of the four Yamanaka factors, but in 2019, Sergiy Velychko , a graduate student in Schöler’s group, found that Oct4 actually wasn’t needed to produce iPSCs. 4 They reported that the reprogramming process took longer, but the resulting cells were of higher quality. They discovered that if they created a more stable Oct4-Sox2 dimer by mutating a residue in Sox2, they could generate more human iPSCs, even from cell types that had been difficult or impossible to reprogram before. Now, other researchers are exploring which parts of Oct4 are most important for reprogramming to potentially create synthetic reprogramming factors as well as looking to artificial intelligence models to further optimize iPSC development. Written by Stephanie DeMarco, PhD Stephanie DeMarco, PhD Stephanie is the Managing Editor at The Scientist . Her background is in parasitology and microbiology. Her work has appeared in Drug Discovery News , Quanta Magazine , and the Los Angeles Times . View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 29, 2026 | 5 min read Save for Later With their labyrinthine chemical structures, macrocyclic peptides can be hard to synthesize, but their structures also make them valuable drug molecules. Image credit: © iStock.com, Artem_Egorov PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 5:00 Share O ften described as “Goldilocks drugs,” macrocyclic peptides are smaller than biologics like antibodies but larger than small molecules. With their just-right size, macrocyclic peptides can travel into spaces too small for biologics to reach and, thanks to their structural rings of amino acids, can target protein-protein interactions that evade small molecules. Researchers at the biopharmaceutical company Merck have taken advantage of macrocyclic peptides’ unique properties to develop enlicitide decanoate (enlicitide), an oral macrocyclic peptide drug that lowers “bad” cholesterol by inhibiting proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9). “PCSK9 inhibitors are known to dramatically improve the outcomes for patients who suffer from cardiovascular disease, but the challenge is all the approved therapies are injectables,” said David Thaisrivongs , executive director, head of biocatalysis at Merck. As potentially the first oral PCSK9 inhibitor, enlicitide could be much more accessible to a wide swath of patients. Merck’s orally delivered macrocyclic peptide drug candidate, enlicitide, inhibits PCSK9, lowering bad cholesterol in people with cardiovascular disease in late-stage clinical trials. Merck & Co., Inc. The only problem is that enlicitide is a very complicated drug to make. “This is a monster of a molecule,” said Alison Narayan , a chemist focused on biocatalysis at the University of Michigan. Stanford Office of Postdoctoral Affairs B ehind every experiment is a long list of routine lab work: refilling tip boxes, sorting samples, cleaning benches, and labeling tubes. While these tasks may seem tedious from the outside, they often bring a surprising sense of calm and accomplishment during stressful days in the lab. Curious to hear which tasks resonated most with researchers, The Scientist asked readers: What’s a mundane lab task that you actually enjoy? Marwa Zafarullah , postdoctoral researcher, Stanford University My favorite mundane task is aliquoting samples from our research participants. There's something almost meditative about the repetition of moving between each tiny tube representing a patient who trusted us with something irreplaceable. For a few quiet minutes, the whole complexity of a multi-omics study distills into me, the pipette, and the sample. Ruth Isenberg studies how gut and oral bacteria wage microscopic battles that shape infection and health. Ruth Isenberg Ruth Isenberg , postdoctoral associate, University of Minnesota, Twin Cities I genuinely enjoy doing mundane chores, like putting caps on culture tubes, racking pipette tips, and unpacking lab supply shipments. When I need a break from thinking, I’ve also been known to start organizing refrigerators and freezers! Rishi Jaiswal , postdoctoral fellow, University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences One mundane lab task I weirdly enjoy is aligning pipette tip boxes after a chaotic experiment—it feels like restoring order to the universe one tip at a time. I also find scanning colony formation assay plates oddly satisfying, especially when the colonies decide to grow in aesthetically pleasing patterns instead of scientific chaos. Rishi Jaiswal combines molecular and structural approaches to uncover how failures in DNA repair drive cancer development. Rishi Kumar Jaiswal Sudheesh Allikka Parambil , associate research scientist, Yale University Every couple of weeks, I thoroughly clean my workspace and lay down a fresh bench protector. It makes me happy! Sudheesh Allikka Parambil explores how RNA regulation enables stem cells to heal, adapt, and protect themselves under stress. Sudheesh Allikka Parambil Georgia Lattanzi , postdoctoral researcher, Salk Institute for Biological Studies I am an early bird, so I am usually in lab by 8:00 or 8:30 a.m. when there are not many people yet. I make my hot coffee, and there is nothing I enjoy more than spending my first hour checking the latest discoveries and reading a few papers and headlines about the immuno-oncology world. Every morning I go through the scientific press and authors' literature to see what's new or how some eminent scientists have shaped their career through their discoveries. It is a ritual that mixes some inspirational approaches with the newest discoveries and gives me the excitement to dive deep into my research. We often minimize the importance of reading science and being up to date with the literature, but going forward in the academic career I think that's one of the key winning factors. It feels like a satisfying reset and a clean close to my work. I also like refilling tip boxes, as it gives me a moment to slow down, rest my mind, and step out of the intense, active focus required during experiments. Opinion Facing the New Reality of NIH Funding New federal policies have created a temporary drop in new NIH awards that is challenging America’s biomedical research community. Written by Harold Collard, MD Harold Collard, MD Harold Collard is the Vice Chancellor for Research and a Professor of Medicine and Health Policy at the University of California, San Francisco. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Mar 20, 2026 | 4 min read Save for Later New processes for awarding grants could lead to delayed or even reduced numbers of researchers being funded. Image credit: ©iStock.com, erhui1979 PDF version Share I n the first three months of 2026, the American biomedical research community has gained much needed clarity regarding the National Institutes of Health’s (NIH’s) funding landscape going forward. In this opinion piece, I describe the general contours of this landscape and some of its key implications—slowdowns and delays in awards, lower success rates for funding, declines in funding opportunities—for NIH–funded researchers. Congressional Support for Biomedical Research Remains Strong On February 3, 2026, President Trump signed into law the “ Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 .” In this bill, Congress rejected the administration’s proposed cuts to NIH and sustained its top-line budget at $47.2 billion. This remarkable decision, coupled with statutory language maintaining federal facilities and administration rates for research agencies at currently negotiated levels, is important to celebrate. It reflects the hard work of Senate and House appropriators and the stalwart bipartisan support in Congress for biomedical research in America. Preserving the top-line budget available to NIH allows the agency to continue supporting new and ongoing research projects from researchers across the country that drive the American biomedical research engine . A significant reduction to NIH’s budget would have been catastrophic: requiring either a near-complete pause in new research awards or the reduction of much of the NIH’s ongoing research. It is not hyperbole to say that Congress saved the NIH and American biomedical research as we know it. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Newsletter updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe The research community has encountered many obstacles over the last year. The issuance of multiple research-related executive orders early in the Trump administration led to a number of challenges for NIH-funded researchers: rapidly evolving NIH policies regarding diversity, equity, and inclusion and other topics; terminations of many existing awards; administrative pauses in foreign collaborations; and a general slowdown in the administrative operations of the agency. Thankfully, most of these challenges have been resolved or greatly improved. This is due to the hard work and advocacy of many stakeholders—researchers, research institutions, professional associations, and elected officials, not to mention the NIH’s staff—in interpreting, navigating, and at times challenging the administration’s policy actions. Unfortunately, there remain two policy changes at the NIH that are causing significant slowdowns and declines in new awards. The first is the transition to the NIH’s new Unified Funding Strategy for new awards, and the second is the transition to multi-year funding for new awards. Changes to NIH’s Policy for New Awards are Causing Slowdowns and Declines The NIH’s Unified Funding Strategy was announced last November. Its core tenets include prioritizing scientific merit, sustaining early career investigators, and promoting “broad distribution and geographic balance of funding, considering the total amount and type of NIH funding already available to each investigator.” The most immediate effect of this strategy is the operational changes in grantmaking it requires from the NIH’s institutes and centers. For example, the policy ended the use of paylines, or funding cutoffs, which many of the institutes and centers relied on for decision-making. Adjusting to a non-payline based funding strategy (not to mention one that now explicitly integrates geographic location and overall funding portfolios for investigators and institutions) is requiring institutes and centers to develop new workflows, which has introduced delays in the award process. While the transition to NIH’s new Unified Funding Strategy is disruptive, the related slowdowns and declines in new awards are likely short-lived. More long-lasting in impact is the second policy change—the transition to multi-year funding for most new NIH awards. The White House’s Office of Management and Budget wants to transition the NIH to a predominantly multi-year funding model, requiring the NIH to obligate the entire cost of most multi-year awards in the year they are awarded. Historically, the NIH has budgeted research dollars for most of its multi-year awards year by year. This meant that future year allocations were obligated with NIH funding appropriated in the relevant future fiscal year. With multi-year funding of awards, the NIH must obligate the full cost of the award (i.e., all years) in the fiscal year the multi-year award is awarded. For example, for a four-year, $250,000 per year R01 award, multi-year funding means that the NIH now needs to obligate $1 million of its current fiscal year dollars to fund this award, as opposed to just $250,000 under the traditional accounting system. This means fewer new awards will be made until the future year obligations from existing, year-by-year funded multi-year awards wash out. Continue reading below... Read More We have already seen the impact of these policy changes, in particular multi-year funding, on the number of new awards NIH has issued. Data from the NIH on their awarded investigator-initiated research grants (i.e., R01-equivalent awards) shows a 24 percent reduction in the number of awards issued from fiscal year 2024 to 2025 (7,720 vs. 5,885), causing the average success rate to drop from 24 percent to 17 percent.  There is little opportunity for a legislative remedy this Congress (e.g., Senate appropriations language further limiting the transition to multi-year funding failed to survive the final FY26 negotiation process) and the current statutory language allows NIH to continue the transition to multi-year funding at the same rate as fiscal year 2025, so we should expect similar numbers and success rates for fiscal year 2027. Investigators and Institutions Need to Adapt The NIH-funded research community needs to recognize the likely scenario of significantly reduced funding of new awards for a period of two to three years. There is no replacing the NIH as the central funder of American biomedical research; private foundations, industry, and philanthropy will not fill this gap. This decline in new NIH awards will undoubtedly result in lost discoveries and innovations , lost jobs, and an accelerated ceding of America’s scientific leadership to other countries that are investing heavily in cutting-edge research. Acute drops in research awards will force innovative researchers to move away from research institutions into private industry or to leave the country for better offers abroad. To survive, individual faculty and institutions will need to proactively identify ways to sustain the scientific workforce and the research programs they support until NIH funding of new awards recovers. Helping investigators to identify and apply for awards from other federal agencies (e.g., Department of Defense, Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, National Science Foundation), private foundations , and industry is a good first step; many NIH-funded scientists do not know much about these alternative sources of funding. Investigators also need to take a careful look at their research programs and plan their projects and budgets with a tighter funding environment in mind. Finally, institutions will need to identify ways to bridge their researchers through this period of reduced funding financially and professionally. This is, by many measures, the proverbial rainy day and institutional leaders should act accordingly. There are many good things happening at the NIH today, and there are many good people at the NIH working tirelessly to support the biomedical research community. Congressional support remains strong, and the NIH is well-funded to continue its mission of advancing fundamental knowledge and enhancing health. However, policy decisions made by this administration—in particular the transition to multi-year funding—have created a period of significantly reduced funding for new awards. We need proactive, investigator and institutional level engagement to sustain science until funding levels improve. Add The Scientist as a preferred Google source to see more of our trusted coverage. Investigators also need to take a careful look at their research programs and plan their projects and budgets with a tighter funding environment in mind. Finally, institutions will need to identify ways to bridge their researchers through this period of reduced funding financially and professionally. This is, by many measures, the proverbial rainy day and institutional leaders should act accordingly. There are many good things happening at the NIH today, and there are many good people at the NIH working tirelessly to support the biomedical research community. Congressional support remains strong, and the NIH is well-funded to continue its mission of advancing fundamental knowledge and enhancing health. Mar 20, 2026 | 4 min read Save for Later New processes for awarding grants could lead to delayed or even reduced numbers of researchers being funded. Image credit: ©iStock.com, erhui1979 PDF version Share I n the first three months of 2026, the American biomedical research community has gained much needed clarity regarding the National Institutes of Health’s (NIH’s) funding landscape going forward. In this opinion piece, I describe the general contours of this landscape and some of its key implications—slowdowns and delays in awards, lower success rates for funding, declines in funding opportunities—for NIH–funded researchers. Congressional Support for Biomedical Research Remains Strong On February 3, 2026, President Trump signed into law the “ Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 .” In this bill, Congress rejected the administration’s proposed cuts to NIH and sustained its top-line budget at $47.2 billion. This remarkable decision, coupled with statutory language maintaining federal facilities and administration rates for research agencies at currently negotiated levels, is important to celebrate. It reflects the hard work of Senate and House appropriators and the stalwart bipartisan support in Congress for biomedical research in America. Preserving the top-line budget available to NIH allows the agency to continue supporting new and ongoing research projects from researchers across the country that drive the American biomedical research engine . A significant reduction to NIH’s budget would have been catastrophic: requiring either a near-complete pause in new research awards or the reduction of much of the NIH’s ongoing research. It is not hyperbole to say that Congress saved the NIH and American biomedical research as we know it. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Newsletter updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe The research community has encountered many obstacles over the last year. The issuance of multiple research-related executive orders early in the Trump administration led to a number of challenges for NIH-funded researchers: rapidly evolving NIH policies regarding diversity, equity, and inclusion and other topics; terminations of many existing awards; administrative pauses in foreign collaborations; and a general slowdown in the administrative operations of the agency. Thankfully, most of these challenges have been resolved or greatly improved. This is due to the hard work and advocacy of many stakeholders—researchers, research institutions, professional associations, and elected officials, not to mention the NIH’s staff—in interpreting, navigating, and at times challenging the administration’s policy actions. Unfortunately, there remain two policy changes at the NIH that are causing significant slowdowns and declines in new awards. The first is the transition to the NIH’s new Unified Funding Strategy for new awards, and the second is the transition to multi-year funding for new awards. Changes to NIH’s Policy for New Awards are Causing Slowdowns and Declines The NIH’s Unified Funding Strategy was announced last November. Its core tenets include prioritizing scientific merit, sustaining early career investigators, and promoting “broad distribution and geographic balance of funding, considering the total amount and type of NIH funding already available to each investigator.” The most immediate effect of this strategy is the operational changes in grantmaking it requires from the NIH’s institutes and centers. For example, the policy ended the use of paylines, or funding cutoffs, which many of the institutes and centers relied on for decision-making. Adjusting to a non-payline based funding strategy (not to mention one that now explicitly integrates geographic location and overall funding portfolios for investigators and institutions) is requiring institutes and centers to develop new workflows, which has introduced delays in the award process. While the transition to NIH’s new Unified Funding Strategy is disruptive, the related slowdowns and declines in new awards are likely short-lived.
